objectives.name: The Seven Layers
objectives.description: The OSI model, encapsulation, and how data moves layer by layer.

items.title: OSI Model — All 7 Layers
rows: HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SSH, DNS, SMTP, SNMP, Telnet
TLS/SSL, JPEG, MPEG, ASCII — encryption & formatting
TCP (reliable), UDP (fast) — port numbers live here
IP, ICMP, OSPF, BGP — Router operates here
Ethernet, 802.11 Wi-Fi, ARP — Switch / MAC addresses
Hubs, cables, repeaters, NICs — raw electrical/optical signals
key_points: Router = Layer 3.  Switch = Layer 2.  Hub = Layer 1.
TCP/UDP port numbers live at Layer 4.
TLS/SSL encryption happens at Layer 6 (Presentation).
Encapsulation adds headers going DOWN (7→1); decapsulation strips them going UP.

items.title: OSI Mnemonic
items.body:
Please  Do  Not  Throw  Sausage  Pizza  Away
  7        6     5      4       3         2        1

(Reversed — bottom to top: All People Seem To Need Data Processing)
key_points: Top-down (app to wire): Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away
Bottom-up (wire to app): All People Seem To Need Data Processing
Exam questions often use BOTH directions — know both.

items.title: Encapsulation & PDU Names
items.body:
When data travels DOWN the OSI stack, each layer ADDS a header (and sometimes a trailer). This is encapsulation.

Layer 7/6/5: Data
Layer 4 adds port numbers → Segment (TCP) or Datagram (UDP)
Layer 3 adds IP header → Packet
Layer 2 adds MAC header + FCS trailer → Frame
Layer 1 converts to bits → Bits on the wire
key_points: Data → Segment → Packet → Frame → Bits  (DSPFB)
De-encapsulation: reverse process on the receiving end.
The Frame Check Sequence (FCS) at Layer 2 detects corruption.
Exam tip: 'What PDU is used at Layer X?' — know DSPFB cold.

rows: Repeats all traffic to all ports
Creates one collision domain — avoid in modern nets
Forwards frames by MAC address (CAM table)
Faster than router for inter-VLAN — no separate router needed
Routes packets between networks using IP
Maintains routing table; connects different network segments
Stateful = tracks connection state; NGFW = Layer 7 inspection
Detects and ALERTS on suspicious traffic

Detects and BLOCKS threats in real time

rows: Cannot validate returning traffic; easy to spoof
App ID, User ID, SSL/TLS decryption, IPS
Higher cost; SSL inspection causes latency
Web traffic only — not a general-purpose firewall
key_points: Stateful FW is the baseline — used everywhere.  Know how it tracks TCP state.
NGFW = stateful + application awareness + SSL inspection + integrated IPS.
WAF specifically protects web apps (SQL injection, XSS, etc.).
The exam may refer to 'stateful packet inspection' — that's a stateful firewall.

items.title: IDS vs IPS — Know the Difference
items.body:
IDS (Intrusion Detection System):
  • Passive — sits on a SPAN port or network tap
  • Sees a copy of traffic (out-of-band)
  • Detects anomalies and sends ALERTS
  • Cannot block traffic — just watches

IPS (Intrusion Prevention System):
  • Active — sits INLINE in the traffic path
  • Processes actual traffic (not a copy)
  • Detects and BLOCKS threats in real time
  • Adds latency; false positives can drop legitimate traffic

HIDS / HIPS = host-based versions running on an endpoint.
key_points: IDS = out-of-band (copy of traffic).  IPS = inline (actual traffic).
IPS can block; IDS cannot — IDS only alerts.
False positive on an IPS = legitimate traffic gets dropped.
HIDS = host-based IDS.  NIDS = network-based IDS.

items.title: Critical Ports — Must Know Cold
rows: Encrypted remote access + secure file transfer
UDP for normal queries; TCP for large/zone transfer
Server listens here — clients broadcast to 255.255.255.255:67
Trivial FTP — unencrypted, used for booting/config files
Email retrieval — downloads and deletes from server
Email retrieval — syncs, keeps on server
Manager → Agent: GET, GETNEXT, SET requests
Virtual Network Computing — cross-platform remote desktop
key_points: FTP = 20 (data) + 21 (control). Both unencrypted.
SSH = 22. SFTP and SCP both tunnel over SSH port 22.
DHCP: server=67, client=68. Both UDP (client has no IP yet → broadcast).
SNMP: polling=161, traps=162. Syslog=514. Know these for monitoring questions.
LDAP=389 (plain), LDAPS=636 (encrypted). Always prefer LDAPS in secure environments.

items.title: Port Memory Tricks
items.body:
Group ports by function to memorize faster:

SECURE vs INSECURE pairs (know both):
  Telnet 23  →  SSH 22 (replacement)
  HTTP 80   →  HTTPS 443 (encrypted)
  LDAP 389  →  LDAPS 636 (encrypted)
  FTP 21    →  SFTP/SCP 22 (over SSH)

EMAIL ports:
  Send: SMTP 25 (server-server), SMTP 587 (client-server w/ auth)
  Receive: POP3 110 (download+delete), IMAP 143 (sync+keep)

NETWORK SERVICES:
  DNS 53 | DHCP 67/68 | TFTP 69

MONITORING:
  SNMP 161/162 | Syslog 514
key_points: When asked about 'secure file transfer' → SFTP (port 22), not FTP (port 21).
When asked about 'unencrypted remote access' → Telnet (23).
Port 587 = SMTP with authentication (for email clients, not relay).
IMAP keeps email on server (sync), POP3 downloads and deletes.

items.title: Essential Port Numbers (memorize cold)
items.body:
Guaranteed exam points — drill until automatic:

  20/21 FTP    22 SSH/SFTP/SCP   23 Telnet    25 SMTP
  53 DNS       67/68 DHCP        69 TFTP      80 HTTP
  110 POP3     123 NTP           143 IMAP     161/162 SNMP
  389 LDAP     443 HTTPS         445 SMB      636 LDAPS
  514 Syslog   3389 RDP          1433 MS-SQL  3306 MySQL
key_points: SSH=22 — SFTP and SCP ride on 22 too. Telnet=23 is its insecure twin.
Secure swaps: HTTP 80->HTTPS 443, LDAP 389->LDAPS 636, FTP->FTPS 990.
DHCP: 67 server / 68 client.  SNMP: 161 queries / 162 traps.
RDP=3389 (Microsoft).  Syslog=UDP 514.  NTP=123.

items.title: IPv4 Address Classes & Special Ranges
rows: RFC 1918 Private — Class B private (172.32+ is PUBLIC)
APIPA — auto-assigned when DHCP fails; link-local only
Limited broadcast — all hosts on local segment
key_points: 172.16–172.31 is private.  172.32.0.0+ is PUBLIC.  This is a common exam trap.
APIPA = 169.254.x.x.  Host with APIPA has no DHCP — cannot reach other networks.
Loopback = 127.0.0.1.  The whole 127.0.0.0/8 is reserved for loopback.
Private addresses are NOT routed on the internet — NAT translates them.

items.title: CIDR Subnet Quick Reference
key_points: Usable hosts = 2^(host bits) − 2.  Subtract network address and broadcast.
/30 = 2 usable hosts.  Perfect for router-to-router point-to-point links.
/26 = 64 addresses, 62 usable.  Important — appears in subnet calculation questions.
Each time you borrow 1 bit: address space halves, number of subnets doubles.

items.title: Subnetting: How to Calculate Fast
items.body:
Given: 192.168.10.75/27 — find the subnet.

Step 1: /27 has 5 host bits → 2^5 = 32 addresses per subnet.

Step 2: Subnet boundaries increment by 32:
  192.168.10.0  (network)  → .31 (broadcast)
  192.168.10.32 (network)  → .63 (broadcast)
  192.168.10.64 (network)  → .95 (broadcast)  ← .75 is in THIS one
  192.168.10.96 (network)  → .127 (broadcast)

Answer: subnet = 192.168.10.64/27

Key formula: Block size = 256 − last octet of subnet mask.
  /27 mask last octet = 224 → Block = 256−224 = 32.
key_points: Block size = 256 − last non-255 octet of subnet mask.
/26 block = 64, /27 block = 32, /28 block = 16, /29 block = 8, /30 block = 4.
Find which block the IP falls in by dividing: 75÷32 = 2 remainder 11 → subnet starts at 64.
First address = network, last address = broadcast.  Both are unusable as host addresses.

items.title: Cloud Service Models (IaaS / PaaS / SaaS)
rows: AWS EC2, Azure VMs, Google Compute Engine
AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Google App Engine, Heroku
Just your data and user access
key_points: Pizza-as-a-Service analogy: IaaS = you cook it; PaaS = restaurant kitchen; SaaS = delivered pizza.
More 'as a Service' = less you manage = less control = less customization.
IaaS gives max control but max responsibility.

items.title: Cloud Deployment Models
rows: Owned by cloud provider (AWS, Azure, GCP)
Low cost, shared resources, least control
Max control, max security, highest cost
Flexible: burst to public, keep sensitive data private
Multiple orgs with shared compliance needs
e.g., Government agencies sharing FISMA infra
key_points: Private cloud = most control + most secure (but costly).
Public cloud = cheapest, least control.
Hybrid = private for sensitive workloads, public for elastic bursting.
Community cloud is often tested as the 'unusual' option — know it.

items.title: NIST 5 Cloud Characteristics
key_points: 1. On-demand self-service — provision resources without human interaction with provider
2. Broad network access — available over the network via standard mechanisms (phone, laptop)
3. Resource pooling — provider serves multiple consumers from shared resources (multi-tenancy)
4. Rapid elasticity — scale up/down quickly; appears unlimited to consumer
5. Measured service — resource use is monitored, controlled, reported (pay-per-use)
items.body:
NIST SP 800-145 defines cloud computing with these 5 essential characteristics. The exam tests whether you can recognize them.

Elasticity = scale resources fast.
Measured service = metered billing.
On-demand = no need to call the provider.

items.title: IPv6 Address Types
rows: Equivalent to 127.0.0.1 in IPv4 — local host
All zeros — equivalent to 0.0.0.0 in IPv4
Auto-configured on every IPv6 interface; not routable — local segment only
Private IPv6 — roughly equivalent to RFC 1918; not globally routed
Publicly routable IPv6 — assigned by IANA/RIRs
Replaces broadcast in IPv6 (no broadcast in IPv6)
Same as unicast — no special range
Single address assigned to multiple interfaces; packet delivered to nearest
key_points: IPv6 has NO broadcast — multicast replaces it (e.g., FF02::1 = all nodes on link).
FE80::/10 = link-local. Every interface gets one automatically. NOT routable.
FC00::/7 = unique local (private). Functionally like RFC 1918 for IPv4.
IPv6 loopback = ::1.  IPv4 loopback = 127.0.0.1.  Know both.

items.title: SDN — Control Plane vs Data Plane
items.body:
Traditional Networking:
  Control plane AND data plane run ON the same physical device (router/switch).
  Each device makes its own routing/forwarding decisions independently.

SDN (Software-Defined Networking):
  CONTROL PLANE → centralized controller (software)
    • Makes all routing/policy decisions
    • Has a global view of the entire network
    • Communicates with switches via OpenFlow or NETCONF

  DATA PLANE → remains on the physical switch
    • Just forwards packets per instructions from controller
    • Dumb hardware — faster forwarding

Benefit: Centralized management, programmable network, faster provisioning.
Use cases: Cloud DCs, SD-WAN, network slicing (5G).
key_points: Control plane = where to send traffic (routing decisions).
Data plane = actually forwarding the packets.
SDN separates them: controller handles control, switches handle forwarding.
OpenFlow = protocol between SDN controller and switches.

items.title: Zero Trust, SASE, and SD-WAN
items.body:
ZERO TRUST ARCHITECTURE (ZTA):
  Core principle: 'Never trust, always verify.'
  • No implicit trust based on network location (inside ≠ trusted).
  • Every request must be authenticated, authorised, and encrypted.
  • Micro-segmentation: fine-grained per-workload security zones.
  • Least-privilege access: users/devices get minimum access needed.

SASE (Secure Access Service Edge):
  Gartner-coined term combining:
    • SD-WAN (network performance)
    • Cloud security (SWG, CASB, ZTNA, FWaaS)
  Delivered as a cloud service — security enforced at the edge.

SD-WAN:
  Intelligently routes traffic across multiple WAN links (MPLS + broadband + LTE)
  based on real-time performance metrics (latency, jitter, packet loss).
  Reduces dependency on expensive MPLS circuits.
key_points: Zero Trust: verify everything, trust nothing by default — even internal traffic.
SASE = SD-WAN + cloud security services in one cloud-delivered package.
SD-WAN optimises WAN by using multiple link types intelligently.
Micro-segmentation = Zero Trust applied inside the data center (stops lateral movement).
ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access) replaces traditional VPN in SASE architecture.

objectives.name: The Layout
objectives.description: Network topologies and data-center architectures.

items.title: Network Topologies Compared
rows: All devices on one shared cable segment
One break = total failure. High collisions. SPOF: the bus cable
Each device connects to two others — forms a loop
One failure takes down ring unless dual-ring. SPOF: any node/link
All devices connect to central hub/switch
SPOF: the central switch (mitigated by redundant switches)
Every device connects to every other
Expensive: n*(n-1)/2 connections. Hard to scale
Flexible — mix star+mesh for key nodes
Direct link between exactly two nodes
Only connects two endpoints — not scalable
key_points: Star = most common LAN topology today (switch at center).
Full mesh = max redundancy, max cost.  Used in WAN/SP core networks.
Bus topology = obsolete.  Ring = used in SONET/SDH (dual-ring).
The internet is a partial mesh — not all routers connect to all routers.

items.title: Data Center: Three-Tier vs Spine-and-Leaf
rows: Spine switches + Leaf switches (2 layers only)
Add a leaf switch = linear scale-out
Avoided — uses ECMP and BGP/EVPN instead
Modern data centers with heavy VM/container traffic
key_points: Three-tier = Core/Distribution/Access.  Collapsed core = Distribution merged into Core.
Spine-and-leaf = any two servers always 2 hops apart.  Predictable latency.
East-West traffic (server↔server) drove adoption of spine-and-leaf in DCs.
North-South = traffic in/out of the DC.  East-West = traffic within the DC.

items.title: Traffic Patterns — North-South vs East-West
items.body:
NORTH-SOUTH traffic:
  Direction: Between external users/internet and servers inside the data center.
  Think of it as traffic crossing the perimeter firewall.
  Example: A user in London browsing a website hosted in AWS.
  Traditional three-tier architecture was designed for this.

EAST-WEST traffic:
  Direction: Between servers WITHIN the same data center.
  Example: Web server → App server → Database server (same DC).
  With virtualization and microservices, this is now the dominant traffic pattern.
  Spine-and-leaf is designed specifically for high east-west volumes.
key_points: East-west traffic dominates modern DCs — it grew with virtualization/microservices.
Spine-and-leaf was invented to handle east-west efficiently.
North-south crosses the perimeter (external ↔ internal).
Exam question: 'server-to-server traffic within a DC' = east-west.

Older ISP/telecom installs — larger than LC
