objectives.name: Pathfinding
objectives.description: Routing protocols, admin distance, NAT, and first-hop redundancy.

items.title: Static vs Dynamic Routing — Printed Directions vs GPS
items.body:
Static = printed directions: fixed route, zero overhead, doesn't adapt if the road closes.
Dynamic = GPS: routers share updates and reroute automatically, at the cost of CPU/bandwidth.

Use static for stub networks, defaults, or backup routes. Use dynamic wherever topology changes or redundancy exists.
key_points: AD = tiebreaker when two sources know the same route — lowest AD wins.
Static AD=1 beats OSPF AD=110 by default.
Mnemonic (low→high AD): Connected(0), Static(1), eBGP(20), EIGRP(90), OSPF(110), RIP(120), iBGP(200).
Floating static route: deliberately set a HIGH AD so it's only a backup.

items.title: Administrative Distance (AD) — Quick Reference
rows: The interface is physically connected — always preferred
Manually configured by admin — almost always preferred over dynamic
Routes learned from external BGP peers (internet routing)
Cisco proprietary — DUAL algorithm, fast convergence
Open standard — link-state, area-based, SPF algorithm
Link-state, used by large ISPs, rarely tested on N+
Distance vector, hop count ≤15, slow convergence — legacy
Routes redistributed INTO EIGRP from another protocol
BGP routes learned from internal BGP peers — least trusted dynamic
Never installed in routing table — effectively blocked
key_points: Lower AD = more trustworthy. Router installs LOWEST AD route.
Static AD=1 almost always beats dynamic protocols (AD 90–200).
Floating static route: set AD > dynamic protocol AD to use as backup only.
Memorise: Connected(0) > Static(1) > eBGP(20) > EIGRP(90) > OSPF(110) > RIP(120) > iBGP(200).
Exam trap: 'Which route is preferred?' — always pick lowest AD.

items.title: Routing Protocols — Head-to-Head
rows: Small legacy networks — avoid in production
Internet routing between ASes — THE internet protocol
Service provider networks, rarely in enterprise
key_points: IGP (Interior) = inside one AS: RIP, EIGRP, OSPF, IS-IS.
EGP (Exterior) = between ASes: BGP (only one in use today).
OSPF area 0 = backbone area — all other areas must connect to area 0.
BGP uses TCP port 179.
OSPF elects DR/BDR on multi-access segments (Ethernet) to reduce LSA flooding.
EIGRP uses RTP (Reliable Transport Protocol) — not TCP/UDP.

items.title: NAT Types — Translation Explained
rows: One-to-one: single private IP ↔ single public IP
Hosting a server — needs consistent public IP
Pool: private IP → one public IP from pool
Multiple clients sharing a pool of public IPs
Many-to-one: all private IPs → one public IP + unique port
Home/office internet access — most common NAT
IPv6-only hosts communicating with IPv4 servers
key_points: PAT (Port Address Translation) = NAT Overload — tracks connections by port number.
Static NAT needed for inbound connections (servers, DMZ hosts).
NAT hides internal addressing — 'inside local' is the private IP.
Inside global = public IP seen by internet. Inside local = private IP on LAN.
NAT breaks end-to-end connectivity (can cause VoIP, VPN, gaming issues).

items.title: First Hop Redundancy Protocols (FHRP)
rows: Hot Standby Router Protocol — most common on Cisco
Gateway Load Balancing Protocol — most advanced, Cisco only
key_points: All FHRPs create a virtual IP + virtual MAC shared by the group.
Clients use the VIRTUAL IP as their default gateway — not a physical router IP.
HSRP: one active, one standby. Election: highest priority wins (default 100); tie → highest IP.
VRRP: same concept as HSRP but RFC standard — compatible with all vendors.
GLBP: one AVG (Active Virtual Gateway) assigns different virtual MACs → true load balancing.
Preemption: when a higher-priority router comes back up, it can reclaim active role (must be enabled in HSRP).

objectives.name: The Switchboard
objectives.description: VLANs, 802.1Q trunking, Spanning Tree, and link aggregation.

items.title: VLAN Fundamentals & 802.1Q Trunking
items.body:
A VLAN (Virtual LAN) is a logical segment of a switched network. It creates separate broadcast domains without needing physical separation.

802.1Q TAGGING:
When a frame travels over a trunk link, an 802.1Q tag (4 bytes) is inserted into the Ethernet header:
  • Tag Protocol ID (TPID): 0x8100
  • Priority (PCP): 3 bits (QoS/CoS)
  • Drop Eligible (DEI): 1 bit
  • VLAN ID (VID): 12 bits → supports 4094 VLANs (0 and 4095 reserved)

PORT MODES:
  • Access port: belongs to ONE VLAN, frames are UNTAGGED
  • Trunk port: carries MULTIPLE VLANs, frames are TAGGED (except native VLAN)
  • Native VLAN: the ONE VLAN that is NOT tagged on a trunk (default VLAN 1 — change it for security)
  • Voice VLAN: access port can carry data VLAN + voice VLAN simultaneously (for IP phones)
key_points: VLANs create separate broadcast domains — a broadcast in VLAN 10 doesn't reach VLAN 20.
Trunk ports tag ALL VLANs except the native VLAN — native VLAN frames pass untagged.
Native VLAN mismatch = security risk (VLAN hopping) — always set native VLAN to unused VLAN.
Default VLAN is VLAN 1 — all ports start in VLAN 1; best practice is to NOT use VLAN 1 for data.
Inter-VLAN routing requires either a router (router-on-a-stick) or a Layer 3 switch (SVI).
DTP (Dynamic Trunking Protocol) — Cisco auto-negotiates trunk; disable on access ports (switchport nonegotiate).

items.title: STP Port States & Roles (802.1D)
key_points: STP convergence = 30–50 seconds total (Blocking→Listening→Learning→Forwarding).
Mnemonic for states: Blocking Learners Listen First — BLLF, or 'Big Losers Listen Forever'.
PORT ROLES: Root Port (toward root bridge), Designated Port (best port on a segment, forwards), Alternate/Backup (blocked to prevent loops).
ROOT BRIDGE: elected by lowest Bridge ID = Bridge Priority (default 32768) + MAC address. Tie: lower MAC wins.
All ports on Root Bridge = Designated (Forwarding).
PortFast: skips Listening/Learning — use on ACCESS ports only (not trunk). Enables immediately.
BPDU Guard: shuts down a PortFast port if it receives a BPDU (protects against accidental switch connections).

items.title: STP Variants & LACP
rows: Original — one spanning tree for all VLANs. Too slow for modern networks.
Rapid STP — same logic, much faster. Backward compatible with 802.1D.
Per-VLAN STP — separate tree per VLAN. Rapid PVST+ uses 802.1w per VLAN.
Maps multiple VLANs to fewer STP instances — scalable in large networks.
Combines multiple physical links into one logical link (EtherChannel/Port-Channel). Active/passive modes.
key_points: RSTP (802.1w) = what you should use today — same concept as STP but < 2 sec convergence.
LACP modes: Active (initiates negotiation) and Passive (responds to negotiation). Active-Active or Active-Passive works; Passive-Passive does NOT.
EtherChannel/Port-Channel: up to 8 active links bundled. STP sees it as ONE logical link — no blocking needed.
LACP vs PAgP: LACP is IEEE standard; PAgP is Cisco proprietary (both do link aggregation).
MSTP groups VLANs into instances — reduces CPU load vs PVST+ in large deployments.

items.title: Inter-VLAN Routing Methods
rows: Single trunk link from switch to router; router uses subinterfaces (one per VLAN)
Simple setup; router becomes bottleneck at high traffic
Switch itself routes between VLANs using Switch Virtual Interfaces
Fast (hardware routing); no external router needed; most scalable
Each VLAN has a dedicated router port
Simple but wastes ports; impractical for many VLANs
key_points: SVI (Switched Virtual Interface) = virtual Layer 3 interface on a switch, one per VLAN.
Router-on-a-stick: connect switch trunk port to router → create subinterfaces with 802.1Q encapsulation.
Layer 3 switch is always preferred in enterprise (line-rate routing, no bottleneck).
Default gateway for hosts in each VLAN = IP address of the SVI or router subinterface for that VLAN.
Exam question: 'Host A (VLAN 10) can't reach Host B (VLAN 20)' → usually missing SVI or misconfigured inter-VLAN routing.

objectives.name: Airwaves
objectives.description: Wireless standards, security protocols, channel planning, and AP architecture.

items.title: 802.11 Wireless Standards — Full Comparison
rows: First 5GHz standard. Less range, no 2.4GHz interference.
First widely adopted. Slow; prone to interference (microwaves, BT).
Backward compatible with 802.11b. Replaced b in most deployments.
MIMO (multiple antennas). Channel bonding to 40 MHz. Dual-band.
MU-MIMO, 80/160 MHz channels, beamforming. Common today.
OFDMA, BSS coloring, TWT (Target Wake Time). Dense environments.
key_points: Memorise: a=5GHz/54M, b=2.4GHz/11M, g=2.4GHz/54M, n=both/600M, ac=5GHz/3.5G, ax=all/9.6G.
802.11ac/Wi-Fi 5 = 5GHz ONLY. Cannot use 2.4GHz band.
Wi-Fi 6E adds the 6GHz band — less congestion, more channels, shorter range.
MIMO (n) = multiple antennas transmit/receive simultaneously on same channel.
MU-MIMO (ac/ax) = Multiple User MIMO — serves multiple clients simultaneously.
OFDMA (ax/Wi-Fi 6) = divides channel into sub-carriers per client — efficient in dense deployments.

items.title: Wireless Security — WEP/WPA/WPA2/WPA3
rows: BROKEN — do not use. IV reuse → cracked in minutes.
Current standard — still widely used and secure.
Strongest — SAE resists offline dictionary attacks.
Encrypts open networks without authentication (WPA3 feature).
key_points: WPA2 Personal = PSK (pre-shared key / passphrase). WPA2 Enterprise = 802.1X + RADIUS server.
WPA3 SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) replaces PSK — prevents offline brute-force attacks.
WPA2 vulnerability: KRACK attack (Key Reinstallation Attack) — mitigated by patches.
802.1X = port-based access control framework. EAP = Extensible Authentication Protocol (runs over 802.1X).
Common EAP types: EAP-TLS (certificate both sides), PEAP (server cert + MSCHAPv2), EAP-FAST.
Captive portal: redirect unauthenticated users to a login page — common in guest Wi-Fi.

items.title: Wireless Channel Planning
items.body:
2.4 GHz BAND:
  • 11 channels in North America (14 worldwide)
  • Channels are 22 MHz wide but spaced 5 MHz apart → OVERLAP
  • Non-overlapping channels: 1, 6, 11 (the only three that don't interfere)
  • All APs in the same area should use channels 1, 6, or 11
  • 2.4 GHz has only 3 non-overlapping channels → congested in dense environments

5 GHz BAND:
  • 24+ non-overlapping 20 MHz channels (varies by country/regulatory domain)
  • Channels can be bonded: 40 MHz (2 channels), 80 MHz (4 channels), 160 MHz (8 channels)
  • DFS (Dynamic Frequency Selection): some 5GHz channels require radar detection + avoidance
  • UNII-1 (indoor), UNII-2 (DFS), UNII-3, UNII-4 sub-bands

6 GHz BAND (Wi-Fi 6E):
  • 59 non-overlapping 20 MHz channels
  • Huge capacity improvement — ideal for dense deployments
key_points: 2.4 GHz non-overlapping: 1, 6, 11 — MEMORISE THIS. Only these three can coexist without interference.
5 GHz has 24+ non-overlapping channels — much less congestion than 2.4 GHz.
Co-channel interference: two APs on same channel → contention (worse than adjacent channel).
Adjacent channel interference: partially overlapping channels (e.g., 1 and 3) → noise floor rises.
Cell sizing: turn down AP power to avoid overlap in dense deployments (smaller cells = more APs needed).
Site survey: walk-through to measure signal strength, noise, and interference before deploying APs.

items.title: AP Architecture & Antenna Types
rows: Fully self-contained — manages own SSID, security, RF. No controller needed. Hard to manage at scale.
Offloads config and management to WLC (Wireless LAN Controller). Uses CAPWAP tunnel to WLC.
Wireless backhaul to other APs — no wired connection to every AP. Extends coverage where cables can't reach.
Connects two wired LAN segments wirelessly — point-to-point or point-to-multipoint.
Radiates 360° horizontally (like a donut shape). Default for most indoor APs. Lower gain (~2–5 dBi).
Focused beam — high gain in one direction. Used for point-to-point links or specific coverage areas.
Extremely high gain, very narrow beam. Long-distance outdoor point-to-point links (up to miles).
Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points — UDP 5246 (control) + 5247 (data). LWAP↔WLC tunnel.
key_points: CAPWAP: lightweight AP tunnels all traffic to WLC. UDP 5246 (control plane) + 5247 (data plane).
WLC (Wireless LAN Controller): centrally manages LWAPs — RF profiles, SSIDs, security, roaming.
Autonomous APs: simple to set up individually; nightmare to manage at scale (each configured separately).
Omnidirectional: good for open office/coverage. Directional: good for hallways, point-to-point outdoor.
EIRP (Effective Isotropic Radiated Power): regulated max transmit power including antenna gain.
SSID can be the same across multiple APs → client roams seamlessly (ESS — Extended Service Set).

objectives.name: Physical Foundations
objectives.description: Data center infrastructure, MDF/IDF, UPS types, and environmental considerations.

items.title: Data Center Hierarchy — MDF, IDF & Cabling
items.body:
WIRING HIERARCHY (3-tier structured cabling):

  Entrance Facility (EF)
       ↓
  Main Distribution Frame (MDF)
       ↓ (vertical/backbone cabling)
  Intermediate Distribution Frame (IDF) — one per floor / wiring closet
       ↓ (horizontal cabling — max 90m)
  Work Area (end devices)

MDF:
  • Houses core/distribution switches, routers, WAN connections, patch panels
  • Central point for the entire building's network
  • Connects to all IDFs via backbone cabling (fiber between floors)

IDF:
  • Floor-level or zone-level wiring closet
  • Houses access layer switches, patch panels
  • Connected to MDF via riser cables (fiber or Cat6A)
  • Contains: switch(es), patch panel, cable management, UPS

HORIZONTAL CABLING (TIA-568):
  • Max 90m permanent link + 10m for patch cables = 100m total
  • Copper (Cat5e/Cat6/Cat6A) — 1000BASE-T up to 100m
  • Fiber for IDF→MDF runs (exceeds copper limit)
key_points: MDF = building's core network hub. IDF = floor/zone distribution point.
Horizontal cabling limit: 90m permanent link + 10m patch = 100m total (TIA-568).
Backbone/vertical cabling connects MDF to IDFs — typically fiber (exceeds 100m copper limit).
66 block (voice/legacy) vs 110 block (data) vs patch panel (modern) — exam knows all three.
Demarcation point (demarc): where ISP's responsibility ends and customer's begins (usually at entrance facility).
Smart jack (NID/NIU): ISP equipment at demarc — tests circuit from ISP side.

items.title: UPS Types & Power Infrastructure
rows: Passes utility power directly; battery + inverter only switch on during outage
Voltage regulator (AVR) adjusts output continuously; battery activates for total failure
Good — handles sags and swells without battery
Always runs through inverter — utility charges battery, inverter powers load 100% of time
Best — clean, regulated, isolated from utility
key_points: Offline UPS: basic and cheap — OK for desktops. NOT suitable for sensitive servers.
Line-Interactive: best value for small server rooms — AVR handles brownouts without depleting battery.
Online (Double Conversion): gold standard for data centers — zero transfer time, cleanest power.
UPS runtime: determined by battery capacity (Ah) vs load (W). More load = shorter runtime.
PDU (Power Distribution Unit): rack-mounted power strip. 'Smart PDU' monitors per-outlet wattage.
Generator: long-term backup power; UPS bridges the gap while generator spins up (~10-30 sec).
Redundant power paths: dual PSUs in servers + separate PDUs on separate UPS/circuits.

items.title: Physical Environment & Data Center Standards
items.body:
HOT AISLE / COLD AISLE (ASHRAE standard):
  • Server racks arranged in alternating rows facing each other
  • Cold aisle: server fronts face each other ← cold air delivered from floor/CRAC unit
  • Hot aisle: server rears face each other → hot exhaust vented to return/ceiling
  • Prevents hot and cold air from mixing → improves cooling efficiency

RACK UNITS:
  • 1U = 1.75 inches of vertical rack space
  • Standard rack = 42U
  • 'Half-depth' servers: 2-post rack (open frame); full-depth servers need 4-post rack

ENVIRONMENTAL MONITORING:
  • Temperature: ASHRAE A2 class = 10°C–35°C (50°F–95°F) for most IT equipment
  • Humidity: 40–60% RH recommended. Too low → ESD risk. Too high → condensation.
  • Environmental sensors alert on temp/humidity out of range

FIRE SUPPRESSION:
  • NEVER water in a server room — use clean agent suppression
  • FM-200 (HFC-227ea): fast, leaves no residue, safe for occupied rooms
  • Halon: replaced by FM-200 (Halon depletes ozone — banned for new installations)
  • CO₂: effective but displaces oxygen — evacuate before activation

PHYSICAL SECURITY:
  • Mantrap (airlock): two doors — only one opens at a time
  • Biometric + badge: multi-factor physical access
  • CCTV: surveillance logging for audit trails
key_points: Hot/cold aisle containment: alternating front-to-front and back-to-back rack rows.
1U = 1.75 inches. Standard rack = 42U (~7 feet). Know this for port density questions.
ASHRAE A2 temperature range: 10°C–35°C — most servers today can tolerate this range.
FM-200 = safe clean agent for occupied server rooms. CO₂ requires evacuation.
ESD (Electrostatic Discharge): risk when humidity too low — ground strap, anti-static mats.
Raised floor: allows underfloor cable management and cold air distribution from CRAC units.

objectives.name: The Power Standard
objectives.description: Power over Ethernet standards, power negotiation, and cable considerations for PoE deployments.

items.title: PoE Power Negotiation & Budgeting
items.body: Power is negotiated between the Powered Device (PD) and the Power Sourcing Equipment (PSE). Management of the total power budget is critical: a switch with a limited budget must account for individual port requirements (e.g., 15.4W/30W) to avoid over-subscription.

items.title: Cable & Infrastructure Considerations
key_points: Cat5e minimum for basic 802.3af (15.4W)
Cat6 or better recommended for longer runs to minimize power loss
Bundle limits: High-wattage PoE can cause heat buildup in large cable bundles
Distance limit: Max run length is 100m; cable resistance reduces available wattage at the end of long runs

objectives.name: The Watchtower
objectives.description: SNMP, syslog, NetFlow, and network monitoring tools.

items.title: SNMP vs Syslog vs NetFlow
rows: Logging errors, logins, and state changes

items.title: SNMP Trap vs Poll
items.body:
A Poll is a 'pull' mechanism: The Management Station (NMS) asks the device for information at set intervals.

A Trap is a 'push' mechanism: The Device (Agent) sends an unsolicited notification to the NMS immediately when a specific condition is met.

items.title: SNMP Versions — v1 vs v2c vs v3
rows: Original standard; GetRequest, SetRequest, GetNextRequest, Trap
Common but insecure — community strings cleartext
AuthNoPriv (auth+no encrypt), AuthPriv (auth+encrypt with AES/DES), NoAuthNoPriv
key_points: SNMPv1/v2c: community string 'public' = read-only, 'private' = read-write. Both cleartext — sniffable.
SNMPv3 AuthPriv mode: authentication (MD5/SHA) + encryption (AES/DES). Use this for production.
SNMP uses UDP 161 for queries (manager → agent), UDP 162 for traps/informs (agent → manager).
Trap = unreliable (fire-and-forget). Inform = reliable (agent retransmits until ACK).
MIB (Management Information Base): database of manageable objects on a device.
OID (Object Identifier): unique numeric address for each MIB object (e.g., 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1 = sysDescr).

items.title: Syslog Severity Levels
rows: Database corruption, loss of backup primary
Disk space low, config change warning
User login, config saved, service started
key_points: Mnemonic: Every Awesome Cisco Engineer Will Need Daily Biscuits (0-7).
Lower number = higher severity. 0 is worst, 7 is most verbose.
Syslog uses UDP 514 (default) or TCP 514/6514 (TLS-secured).
Syslog server (collector): centralised log aggregation — Graylog, Splunk, syslog-ng.
Severity 0-3: critical/alerts requiring immediate attention.
Production devices usually set to level 5 (Notice) or 6 (Info) — level 7 (Debug) floods logs.

items.title: Network Monitoring Tools Comparison
rows: Device health: CPU, memory, interface counters, config
Traffic flows: src/dst IP, port, protocol, bytes
Bandwidth analysis, traffic patterns, anomaly detection
Network traffic stats captured at remote devices
Detailed traffic analysis without centralised polling
Full packet capture from a switch port
Packet analysis with Wireshark; IDS sensors
key_points: NetFlow = flow-level visibility (who talked to whom, how much). SNMP = device-level stats.
SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) / port mirroring: copies traffic from source port to monitor port for analysis.
RSPAN (Remote SPAN): mirrors traffic across the network to a remote switch port.
Baseline: record normal performance metrics to compare against anomalies later.
NMS (Network Management System): software platform that uses SNMP to monitor/manage all devices.
Nagios, PRTG, SolarWinds, Zabbix — common NMS platforms.

objectives.name: The Metrics Chamber
objectives.description: Network performance metrics, QoS, and interface error diagnostics.

items.title: Network Performance Metrics
rows: Maximum data transfer capacity of a link
Lower than expected = overhead, errors, congestion
Time for a packet to travel from source to destination
Variation in latency between consecutive packets
Percentage of packets that fail to reach destination
key_points: VoIP quality thresholds: latency <150ms, jitter <30ms, packet loss <1%.
Bandwidth ≠ throughput. Bandwidth is the pipe size; throughput is actual water flowing.
Jitter buffer: VoIP devices use a small buffer to smooth out jitter — too large = latency, too small = choppy.
Packet loss causes TCP to trigger congestion control (slow start) — dramatically reduces throughput.
Establish a BASELINE of normal metrics — anomaly detection compares current vs baseline.

items.title: QoS — Differentiated Services & Queuing
rows: Marks IP packets for priority treatment. EF=46 (VoIP), AF classes, CS classes, BE=0 (default)
VLAN-tagged frames only. 7=highest priority. Mapped to DSCP at L3 boundary.
Buffers excess traffic — introduces delay but avoids drops
Drops or re-marks excess traffic immediately — no buffering
Guarantees VoIP/real-time traffic is always served first
Assigns minimum bandwidth guarantee per traffic class
key_points: DSCP EF (Expedited Forwarding) = 46 — used for VoIP/real-time traffic (strict priority).
DSCP BE (Best Effort) = 0 — default, no special treatment.
Shaping vs Policing: shaping queues excess (smooth, adds delay). Policing drops excess (harsh, immediate).
QoS must be configured end-to-end — a single device without QoS breaks the chain.
Voice traffic: mark at ingress (access port), trust DSCP at core, use LLQ for guaranteed forwarding.

items.title: Interface Errors & Diagnostics
rows: Frames < 64 bytes — collision or malformed frames
Check for collisions, duplex mismatch, or faulty NIC
Check for jumbo frame misconfiguration or MTU mismatch
Corrupt frames — bad cable, connector, or interference
Replace cable, check SFP/connector, test cable with tester
Drops due to buffer overflow or hardware issues
Check interface utilisation — possible upgrade needed
One end full-duplex, other half-duplex → collisions and errors
Set both ends to same duplex explicitly — disable auto-negotiate
Check cable, SFP, remote port, or spanning tree issue
key_points: Duplex mismatch: most common cause of CRC errors + late collisions on Ethernet links.
Auto-negotiate: can fail — best practice is explicit speed/duplex on server and uplink ports.
Late collisions (detected >512 bits into frame) = strong indicator of duplex mismatch.
show interface: key command to see all error counters on Cisco devices.
Runts + collisions together = typical half-duplex or duplex mismatch scenario.

items.title: Traffic Shaping vs Policing — The On-Ramp Meter vs The Speed Trap
items.body:
Shaping = on-ramp metering light: holds excess traffic in a queue and releases it at a steady rate. Nothing dropped, but adds delay.
Policing = speed trap: excess traffic is dropped or re-marked instantly. No delay, but causes loss/retransmits.

Both use a token bucket — traffic within the bucket passes normally, traffic beyond it is queued (shaping) or dropped (policing).
key_points: Shaping: queue + delay, no loss — used outbound toward a slower link.
Policing: drop/re-mark, no delay — used inbound to enforce a contracted rate (e.g., ISP CIR).
Shaping smooths bursts; policing protects the network from a sender exceeding its rate.

objectives.name: The Archives
objectives.description: Network documentation, change management, and organizational policies.

items.title: Network Diagram Types
rows: Network topology, IP addressing, VLANs, routing
IP subnets, routers, switches, VLANs, cloud symbols
Troubleshooting, capacity planning, understanding traffic flow
Actual physical layout of equipment and connections
Exact device locations, cable types, port numbers
Cable runs, patch panel mappings, port-to-port
Cable IDs, patch panel labels, wall jack locations
Rack unit layout — what's installed where in each rack
Device model, U position, PDU, cable management
Traffic flows, bandwidth utilization at normal operation
key_points: Logical ≠ Physical: two devices can be adjacent logically but floors apart physically.
Documentation is a living document — update after every change.
IP address management (IPAM): software or spreadsheet tracking all assigned IPs, subnets, DNS.
Out-of-date documentation is worse than no documentation — it misleads troubleshooting.
Rack diagram should include power draw (W per device) to prevent PDU/UPS overload.

items.title: Change Management Process
items.body:
Change management ensures network changes are planned, reviewed, and reversible — reducing outages from uncontrolled changes.

KEY STEPS:
  1. RFC (Request for Change): document the change, reason, scope, schedule, rollback plan
  2. CAB (Change Advisory Board): reviews and approves/rejects the RFC
  3. Change window: scheduled maintenance period (often low-traffic hours)
  4. Implementation: execute the change following the documented procedure
  5. Testing: verify the change works as expected
  6. Rollback: revert using the documented rollback plan if something breaks
  7. Documentation update: update diagrams, IP docs, configs after successful change

CHANGE TYPES:
  • Standard change: pre-approved, low risk, recurring (e.g., adding a user)
  • Normal change: requires RFC + CAB approval
  • Emergency change: expedited process for critical issues (post-change documentation still required)
key_points: Every change needs a rollback plan — know how to undo it before you start.
Change window: schedule during low-impact hours (nights/weekends for business networks).
CAB (Change Advisory Board): committee that evaluates risk and approves changes.
Emergency changes: still document after the fact — 'fix first, document second'.
Configuration backups: always back up device config BEFORE making changes.
RFC must include: reason, scope, risk assessment, test plan, rollback plan, schedule.

items.title: Policies and Agreements
rows: Defines permitted use of org network/systems
Users must sign; covers internet use, prohibited content, personal device use
Rules for personal devices on corp network
MDM enrollment, network segmentation (guest VLAN), data containerisation
Protects confidential info shared with third parties
Vendors, contractors, employees — legal agreement before access
Defines service expectations between provider and customer
Uptime % (e.g., 99.9%), response time, MTTR, remedies for breach
Monitors email, USB, cloud upload for sensitive data (PII, PCI, PHI)
Less binding than SLA — used between internal departments or partners
key_points: SLA 99.9% uptime = ~8.76 hours downtime/year. 99.99% = ~52.6 min/year. 99.999% = ~5.26 min/year.
BYOD risk: personal devices may lack corporate security controls — use network segmentation.
MDM (Mobile Device Management): enforce policies, remote wipe, containerise corp data on personal devices.
PII = Personally Identifiable Information. PHI = Protected Health Information (HIPAA). PCI = Payment Card data.
DLP can be endpoint-based (agent) or network-based (proxy/CASB).

items.title: Change Management Order — "Rita Cooks Wonderful Indian Tacos, Daily"
items.body:
"Rita Cooks Wonderful Indian Tacos, Daily" = the change order:
Rita=RFC (request, scope, rollback plan) → Cooks=CAB (approves) → Wonderful=Window (maintenance time) → Indian=Implementation → Tacos=Testing → Daily=Documentation.

If Implementation/Testing fails, ROLLBACK happens before Documentation.
key_points: Standard change = pre-approved, low-risk, skips full CAB.
Normal change = full RFC + CAB cycle (the mnemonic above).
Emergency change = fix first, document/CAB after.
Always back up config BEFORE implementing — gives rollback something to restore.

objectives.name: The Vault
objectives.description: High availability, RAID, NIC teaming, clustering, and redundancy design.

items.title: RAID Levels — Quick Reference
rows: None — any disk failure = total loss
Fastest but zero redundancy. Not for important data.
Exact copy on second disk. Usable capacity = 50%.
Most common. Usable = N-1 disks. Slow rebuild.
Safer than RAID 5 for large arrays. Usable = N-2 disks.
key_points: RAID 5: most common for file servers — balance of performance, capacity, fault tolerance. CANNOT survive 2 disk failures.
RAID 6: preferred for large drives (>2TB) where rebuild time increases second failure risk.
RAID 10: best for databases/high I/O — can lose one disk per mirrored pair (possibly multiple).
RAID 0: NEVER for production data — zero fault tolerance.
RAID is NOT a backup — it protects against drive failure, not accidental deletion, ransomware, or site disaster.
Hot spare: idle disk automatically rebuilds when a RAID member fails.

items.title: High Availability Concepts
rows: All nodes actively process traffic simultaneously — load balanced
Two web servers both serving requests; traffic split between them
One node active, one on standby — standby takes over on failure
Primary DB server + standby DB; standby activates only on failure
Multiple NICs aggregated into one logical interface
Two 1Gbps NICs bonded = 2Gbps + redundancy; one NIC fails → other carries on
Multiple physical paths to a storage device (SAN)
iSCSI with two HBAs — if one path fails, traffic uses alternate path automatically
Two ISP connections via different paths — if one fails, other carries traffic
System continues at reduced capacity after partial failure
RAID 5 array after 1 disk failure — still operates (degraded) until disk replaced
key_points: Active-Active: all nodes share load → better performance AND redundancy.
Active-Passive: standby wastes resources when idle, but simpler to configure.
NIC teaming modes: Active-Backup (failover only), LACP 802.3ad (active-active + bonding), Round-Robin.
Single point of failure (SPOF): any component whose failure takes down the system — eliminate via redundancy.
Five 9s (99.999%) availability = ~5 minutes downtime/year — requires HA at every layer.
Load balancer: distributes requests to server pool — can do health checks and remove failed servers.

items.title: Parity — One Disk of Math, Not Data
items.body:
Parity = checksum (XOR) across all data disks in a stripe. Takes ~1 disk of capacity, any array size. Lose 1 disk → parity + survivors rebuild it.

'Distributed' = parity rotates across all disks (no bottleneck).
key_points: RAID 5 = 1 parity block → survives 1 disk failure.
RAID 6 = 2 parity blocks (P+Q) → survives 2 disk failures.
Rebuild reads ALL surviving disks — long rebuild = 2nd-failure risk.

objectives.name: The Recovery Room
objectives.description: Disaster recovery sites, backup strategies, RTO, RPO, MTTR, and MTBF.

items.title: Disaster Recovery Site Types
rows: Just space, power, cooling — NO equipment
Partially equipped — servers present but not fully configured
Fully operational mirror — identical equipment, live data sync
key_points: Hot site: most expensive but fastest failover — data is always current (continuous replication).
Cold site: cheapest — just floor space and power. Requires shipping equipment and full restore.
Warm site: middle ground — hardware present but needs config + data restore.
Cloud DR / DRaaS (Disaster Recovery as a Service): spin up virtual infrastructure in cloud on demand.
Geographic diversity: DR site should be far enough to avoid same regional disaster (hurricane, earthquake).
Test your DR plan regularly — an untested DR plan may fail when needed.

items.title: Backup Types Comparison
rows: ALL data regardless of change flag
Only data changed since LAST backup (full OR incremental)
Slowest (need full + all incrementals in sequence)
Full backup + ALL incrementals since full
All data changed since last FULL backup
key_points: Incremental: fast to back up, slow to restore (need full + every incremental in order).
Differential: slower to back up each day (grows), but only need last full + last diff to restore.
3-2-1 rule: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite.
Backup window: time allowed for backup operation — incrementals fit tighter windows.
Backup rotation schemes: GFS (Grandfather-Father-Son) — daily/weekly/monthly retention tiers.
Test restores regularly — backup files that cannot be restored are worthless.

items.title: RTO, RPO, MTTR, MTBF
rows: Maximum acceptable time to restore service after a disaster
Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time (how old can the backup be?)
Average time to repair/restore a failed component
Average time between failures of a component or system
key_points: RTO: 'How long can we be down?' — drives DR site choice. RTO=0 → hot site. RTO=days → cold site.
RPO: 'How much data can we lose?' — drives backup frequency. RPO=1hr → backup every hour.
RPO 4 hours + incremental every 4 hours: if disaster strikes, worst case = 4 hours of data lost.
MTBF: used to predict reliability. Higher MTBF = more reliable. Used for redundancy planning.
MTTR: drives support contract choices (4-hour hardware replacement SLA = MTTR ≤ 4 hours).
Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR) — increasing MTBF or decreasing MTTR improves availability.

items.title: GFS Backup Rotation — The Family Tree of Backup Sets
items.body:
GFS (Grandfather-Father-Son) = 3-tier backup retention.
Son = daily, kept days. Father = weekly, kept ~a month. Grandfather = monthly, kept ~a year (often offsite).

Key idea: PROMOTION — the same daily job is just retained longer on certain days, not run 3x.
key_points: Balances storage cost vs how far back you can restore.
Grandfather (monthly) tapes are best candidates for offsite/cold storage.
Works with any backup type underneath (full/incremental/differential).
Test restores from each tier — an untested grandfather tape is worthless.

objectives.name: The Threat Landscape
objectives.description: Attack types, social engineering, DDoS categories, and threat actors.

items.title: Attack Types — Identification & Mitigation
rows: Single attacker floods target with traffic or exploits vulnerability to exhaust resources
Rate limiting, firewall ACLs, null routing attack source
Botnet of thousands of compromised hosts floods target simultaneously
Anti-DDoS scrubbing service (Cloudflare, AWS Shield), upstream filtering
Attacker positions between two hosts — intercepts and optionally modifies traffic
Encrypt all traffic (TLS/IPsec), certificate pinning, mutual authentication
Attacker sends gratuitous ARPs to map victim IPs to attacker's MAC — intercepts LAN traffic
Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI), static ARP entries for critical hosts
Corrupt DNS cache or intercept DNS responses — redirect users to malicious sites
DNSSEC, encrypted DNS (DoH/DoT), use trusted resolvers
Attacker runs unauthorised DHCP server — assigns malicious default gateway/DNS
DHCP snooping — designate trusted DHCP ports only
Attacker sets up fake AP with same SSID — users connect, traffic intercepted
802.1X Enterprise auth (rogue can't replicate), wireless IDS, RF monitoring
Attacker sends spoofed deauth frames to disconnect clients from legitimate AP
Double-tagging or DTP exploit to jump to another VLAN
Change native VLAN, disable DTP, use dedicated unused native VLAN
Attacker captures and retransmits valid authentication traffic
Session tokens, timestamps, nonces in authentication protocols
Try a few common passwords against many accounts — avoids lockout thresholds
Account lockout after N attempts, MFA, strong password policy
Systematically try all possible passwords against one account
Account lockout, MFA, long complex passwords, rate limiting
Pre-computed hash-to-plaintext lookup table for cracking password hashes
Salt passwords before hashing — salting defeats rainbow tables entirely
key_points: ARP poisoning → On-path/MITM at Layer 2. Mitigation: DAI (Dynamic ARP Inspection).
DNS poisoning → redirect at Layer 7. Mitigation: DNSSEC validates DNS responses cryptographically.
Rogue DHCP → gives clients malicious gateway. Mitigation: DHCP snooping (trust only uplink port).
Evil twin vs rogue AP: rogue = unauthorised AP on your network. Evil twin = fake AP mimicking your SSID.
DDoS types: Volumetric (bandwidth flood), Protocol (SYN flood, Smurf — exploits L3/L4), Application (HTTP flood, Slowloris — L7).
Salt defeats rainbow tables — even same passwords produce different hashes per-user.

items.title: Social Engineering Attacks
rows: Mass email impersonating trusted entity — generic, sent to many
Fake PayPal email asking all users to 'verify account'
Targeted phishing — researched and personalised for specific victim
Email to CFO from 'CEO' requesting urgent wire transfer
Fake legal subpoena email sent to CEO
Voice/phone phishing — caller impersonates IT helpdesk, bank, IRS
'This is Microsoft Support — your PC is infected, give us access'
SMS phishing — text message with malicious link or pretexting
Text: 'Your package is held — click here to confirm delivery'
Creating a fabricated scenario to extract information
Attacker pretends to be an auditor needing network credentials
Following an authorised person through a secured door without authenticating
Attacker carries boxes and walks in behind badge-access employee
Leaving infected USB drives in visible locations for victims to plug in
USB labelled 'Payroll Q4 2024' left in company car park
key_points: Phishing is generic (mass). Spear phishing is targeted. Whaling targets executives specifically.
Vishing = Voice. Smishing = SMS. Phishing = Email. Know the prefix.
Social engineering exploits HUMANS, not technology — technical controls don't fully prevent it.
Key defence: security awareness training — users recognise and report attempts.
Pretexting = the story the attacker tells to justify their request for access/info.
Tailgating defence: mantrap/airlock, badge + PIN, security awareness training to challenge strangers.

items.title: DDoS Attack Categories & Threat Actors
rows: Overwhelm bandwidth — huge traffic volume (Gbps scale)
UDP flood, ICMP flood, DNS amplification
Exhaust state tables on firewalls/routers — not just bandwidth
SYN flood (half-open TCP connections), Smurf attack
Exhaust server resources with seemingly valid requests
HTTP GET flood, Slowloris (holds connections open), DNS query flood
Government-sponsored, highly skilled, long-term APT campaigns
Ideologically motivated — embarrass or disrupt target
Current or former employee with legitimate access
Disgruntled employee exfiltrating data or sabotaging systems
Low skill — uses existing tools/exploits without understanding them
Runs downloaded DDoS tools against targets
Financially motivated — ransomware, data theft, fraud
key_points: DNS amplification: small query → large response sent to spoofed victim IP. Amplification factor up to 50x.
SYN flood: send many SYN packets without completing handshake — exhausts server's half-open connection table.
Mitigation for SYN flood: SYN cookies (server doesn't allocate state until handshake complete).
APT (Advanced Persistent Threat): long-term, stealthy compromise — often nation-state sponsored.
Insider threat: hardest to detect — has legitimate credentials. Defence: least privilege, DLP, audit logs.
Script kiddies: unsophisticated but can still cause damage with off-the-shelf tools.

items.title: Threat Actor Mnemonic — "Sneaky Hackers Inside Often Attack"
items.body:
Sneaky Hackers Inside Often Attack = the 5 threat actor types:
Script kiddie → low skill, downloaded tools, no real motive.
Hacktivist → ideology, wants to be SEEN.
Insider → already has access — hardest to detect.
Organized crime → money (ransomware, fraud).
APT/nation-state → patient, stealthy, long-term access.
key_points: Hacktivist wants visibility; APT wants the opposite — long-term stealth.
Insider threats are hard to catch because the access itself isn't suspicious.
Sophistication/resourcing roughly increases left→right in the mnemonic.
Quickest exam tell-apart: ideology vs money vs espionage.

items.title: CIA Triad + AAA (know both trios cold)
items.body:
CIA Triad — the security goals:
  Confidentiality - only authorized eyes (encryption)
  Integrity       - data unaltered (hashing)
  Availability    - reachable when needed (redundancy)

AAA — access control:
  Authentication - WHO are you?  (password, MFA)
  Authorization  - what may you DO? (permissions)
  Accounting     - what DID you do? (logging/audit)
key_points: Authentication = identity; Authorization = permissions. The exam mixes these on purpose.
TACACS+ encrypts the WHOLE packet and separates AuthN/AuthZ; RADIUS encrypts only the password.
Hashing protects Integrity; Encryption protects Confidentiality.
Accounting/Auditing = the logs proving who did what.

objectives.name: The Perimeter Wall
objectives.description: Firewalls, IDS/IPS, DMZ, network segmentation, and Zero Trust architecture.

items.title: Firewall Types — Full Comparison
rows: Src/Dst IP, port, protocol per packet
Cannot validate return traffic; easily spoofed
App ID, User ID, SSL decryption, IPS, threat intel
Higher cost; SSL inspection adds latency; complex config
Web traffic only — not general purpose
FW + IPS + AV + Web filter + VPN + DLP in one box
Single point of failure; performance impact; SMB-focused
key_points: Stateless = no memory of connections. Stateful = tracks session state (syn/established/fin).
NGFW adds App-ID (identifies app regardless of port) and User-ID beyond stateful.
WAF: specifically defends web apps against SQLi, XSS, path traversal — placed in front of web servers.
UTM: one appliance for everything — cost-effective for small business but can bottleneck.
Implicit deny: firewall drops anything not explicitly permitted. Always the last rule.
DMZ: screened subnet between two firewalls — public-facing servers here (web, mail, DNS).

items.title: IDS vs IPS and Network Segmentation
rows: DETECTS and ALERTS — passive, out-of-band or tap mode
Cannot block traffic. False positive = alert on legitimate traffic. No latency added.
DETECTS and BLOCKS — active, inline mode
Sits in the traffic path. False positive = drops legitimate traffic. Adds small latency.
Host-based IDS/IPS — agent installed on endpoint
Monitors OS calls, file changes, running processes on the host itself.
Screened subnet between untrusted internet and trusted internal network
Public-facing servers (web, email, DNS) placed here. Internet can reach DMZ; DMZ cannot initiate to internal.
Synonym for DMZ — subnet accessible from both internet and internal, but restricted
Typically between two firewalls: external FW faces internet, internal FW protects LAN.
Decoy system designed to attract attackers — logs their techniques
No real data. Alerts admins to active intrusion attempts. Honeynets = multiple honeypots.
Hardened, audited gateway to reach sensitive internal systems
Admins connect to bastion first, then SSH/RDP from there to internal servers.
Granular network segmentation — per-workload firewall policies (East-West traffic control)
Software-defined; used in data centres/cloud. Limits lateral movement if one host is compromised.
key_points: IDS = detect only. IPS = detect + block. IPS must be inline; IDS can be tap/span.
IPS false positive risk: blocks legitimate traffic — tune signatures carefully.
DMZ: two-firewall design — outer FW (internet→DMZ), inner FW (DMZ→LAN). Only DMZ servers are reachable from internet.
Honeypot: zero legitimate traffic expected — any access = suspicious. High signal-to-noise ratio for alerts.
Zero Trust: 'never trust, always verify' — no implicit trust based on network location. Every access request authenticated/authorized.
Defense in depth: multiple overlapping security layers — compromising one layer doesn't mean full compromise.

items.title: The DMZ Sandwich — Two-Firewall Design
items.body:
Internet → FW1 → DMZ (web/mail/DNS servers) → FW2 → Internal LAN.
DMZ = the filling — reachable from outside, but can't freely reach the LAN.
FW1: only DMZ-bound traffic gets in. FW2: only specific DMZ→LAN flows allowed (e.g., web server → DB on one port).
key_points: If a DMZ server is compromised, FW2 still blocks it from roaming the LAN.
Single-firewall DMZ = a third interface/zone on one device — same logic, less redundancy.
Public-facing servers (web, mail, DNS) live in the DMZ — never the internal LAN.
Implicit deny on both firewalls — only explicitly permitted flows pass.

items.title: Attack Types — fast categorization
items.body:
Group attacks by what they abuse:

  Spoofing / on-path: ARP spoofing, MAC spoofing, MITM, DNS poisoning, rogue DHCP/AP
  Denial:             DoS, DDoS, amplification/reflection
  Social engineering: phishing, vishing, tailgating, shoulder surfing
  Wireless:           evil twin, deauth, jamming
  Reconnaissance:     port scan, war-driving
key_points: ARP spoofing maps the attacker's MAC to the gateway's IP -> on-path interception.
Evil twin = rogue AP imitating a legit SSID to harvest credentials.
Amplification (DNS/NTP) turns a tiny request into a huge response aimed at the victim.
Deauth attack kicks clients off Wi-Fi - often the setup for an evil twin.

objectives.name: The Secret Tunnels
objectives.description: VPN technologies, IPsec modes, SSL/TLS, PKI, and cryptographic concepts.

items.title: VPN Types — Site-to-Site vs Remote Access
rows: Permanently connect two office networks over internet
Router/firewall handles VPN — transparent to end users. Always-on.
Individual users connect to corporate network from anywhere
Client software on endpoint. User authenticates to connect.
Works through firewalls (port 443 usually open). Clientless option via browser.
More complex setup. Better performance. Blocked by some firewalls (UDP 500/4500).
No encryption by default — combine with IPsec for security.
Only corporate traffic goes through VPN — internet goes direct
Reduces VPN load but internet traffic bypasses corporate security controls.
key_points: SSL/TLS VPN advantage: uses HTTPS port 443 — rarely blocked by firewalls. Easy for remote users.
IPsec advantage: stronger performance for site-to-site. Uses UDP 500 (IKE), UDP 4500 (NAT traversal).
Full tunnel: ALL traffic through VPN (including internet) — more secure but higher load on VPN gateway.
Split tunnel: only LAN traffic through VPN — internet bypasses VPN. Security risk: endpoint not protected by corporate controls.
GRE alone = no security. GRE + IPsec = encrypted tunnel that can carry routing protocols.
Always-on VPN: endpoint is always connected to corporate network — reduces attack surface on remote devices.

items.title: IPsec — Protocols, Modes, and Key Exchange
rows: IP protocol 51. Verifies packet was not tampered with. Does NOT hide content.
IP protocol 50. Encrypts payload. Used in almost all deployments.
Encrypts payload only — original IP header preserved
Used for host-to-host VPNs. Endpoints must be VPN endpoints.
Encrypts entire original packet + adds new outer IP header
Used for network-to-network (site-to-site) VPNs. Standard for most VPNs.
Establishes secure channel for Phase 2 negotiation. Diffie-Hellman key exchange.
Creates ISAKMP SA (management tunnel). Main mode (6 msgs) or Aggressive mode (3 msgs).
Negotiates the actual IPsec tunnel parameters (encryption, hashing, lifetime)
Creates IPsec SA (data tunnel). Uses PFS optionally.
New Diffie-Hellman exchange for each session — compromise of one key doesn't expose others
Prevents decryption of past sessions if long-term keys are later compromised.
key_points: AH = integrity only (no encryption). ESP = encryption + integrity. Use ESP.
Transport mode: encrypt payload only (host-to-host). Tunnel mode: encrypt entire packet (network-to-network).
IKE Phase 1 = management tunnel (authenticate peers). Phase 2 = data tunnel (IPsec SA).
UDP 500 = IKE/ISAKMP. UDP 4500 = IPsec NAT traversal (encapsulates ESP in UDP).
DH (Diffie-Hellman): allows two parties to establish shared secret over insecure channel. Basis of IKE.
PFS: use it. Without PFS, compromise of the long-term key can decrypt ALL past traffic.

items.title: PKI, Certificates, and Encryption
rows: Framework for issuing, managing, and revoking digital certificates
Enables trust in public keys via chain of trust to a trusted CA.
Trusted entity that signs and issues digital certificates
Root CA → Intermediate CA → End-entity cert. Root CA self-signed.
Binds a public key to an identity, signed by CA
Contains: subject, issuer, public key, validity period, SAN, serial number.
Request submitted to CA containing public key + identity info
CA signs the CSR → issues certificate. Private key never leaves the requester.
Published list of revoked certificate serial numbers
Checked by clients to detect revoked certs. Can be stale — updated periodically.
Client queries OCSP responder for cert status: good/revoked/unknown. Faster than CRL.
Same key encrypts and decrypts — fast
AES-128/256 (block cipher). Used for bulk data encryption.
Public key encrypts; private key decrypts (or vice versa for signatures)
RSA, ECC. Slower. Used for key exchange, signatures, certificates.
Protocol securing communications — record protocol + handshake protocol
TLS 1.3 current standard. Negotiates cipher suite, exchanges keys, authenticates server (and optionally client).
key_points: TLS handshake: client hello → server hello + cert → client verifies cert → key exchange → symmetric session key established.
Certificate chain: trust flows Root CA → Intermediate CA → End-entity cert. Root CA must be trusted by client.
CRL vs OCSP: CRL = list (download whole list). OCSP = per-cert query (real-time, more efficient).
OCSP stapling: server fetches OCSP response and 'staples' it to TLS handshake — client doesn't need to query OCSP separately.
AES (symmetric) for bulk data. RSA/ECDH (asymmetric) for key exchange. Hybrid approach used in TLS.
Self-signed certificate: signed by same entity that issued it — not trusted by others without explicit import.

items.title: AH vs ESP — "AH, No Hiding"
items.body:
AH (Authentication Header) = "AH, no hiding" — integrity + auth only, payload stays in cleartext. IP protocol 51.
ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) = Encrypts, Seals, Protects — encryption + integrity + auth. IP protocol 50.

Almost every real deployment uses ESP.
key_points: AH provides NO confidentiality — that's the whole mnemonic.
ESP is the one that actually encrypts the payload.
Protocol numbers: AH=51, ESP=50 — both ride directly on IP, not TCP/UDP.
Tunnel mode (whole packet) vs transport mode (payload only) applies to both.

objectives.name: The Gatehouse
objectives.description: AAA, RADIUS, TACACS+, 802.1X, NAC, port security, DHCP snooping, DAI, and ACLs.

items.title: AAA — RADIUS vs TACACS+
rows: Combines Authentication + Authorization in one response
key_points: RADIUS = UDP, encrypts only password. TACACS+ = TCP, encrypts everything.
RADIUS best for network access (802.1X, VPN). TACACS+ best for device admin (SSH to router).
AAA: Authentication (who are you?), Authorization (what can you do?), Accounting (what did you do?).
RADIUS ports: UDP 1812 (auth) / 1813 (accounting). Old: 1645/1646. Know both.
TACACS+ TCP 49. TCP = reliable delivery — important for device management sessions.
EAP runs over 802.1X — RADIUS is the backend that processes EAP authentication.

items.title: Layer 2 Security — DHCP Snooping, DAI, Port Security
rows: Designates switch ports as 'trusted' (uplink to real DHCP server) or 'untrusted' (access ports). DHCP offers on untrusted ports are dropped.
Uses DHCP snooping binding table to validate ARP packets. ARP replies on untrusted ports checked — invalid = dropped.
Validates source IP on untrusted ports against DHCP snooping binding table. Prevents hosts from spoofing another host's IP.
Limits number of MAC addresses on an access port. Violation modes: Protect (drop), Restrict (drop + log), Shutdown (err-disable port).
Port security variant — first learned MAC is stored in config automatically. Only that MAC allowed unless manually changed.
Rate-limits broadcast, multicast, or unicast traffic per port. Activates when threshold exceeded (drops or shuts port).
key_points: DHCP snooping must be enabled BEFORE DAI — DAI relies on the DHCP snooping binding table.
Port security violation modes: Protect (silent drop), Restrict (drop + SNMP alert), Shutdown (err-disable — port goes down). Default = Shutdown.
Sticky MAC: learned dynamically but saved to running-config. Survives reboot if saved to startup-config.
DAI: all ports untrusted by default — only trunk/uplink ports should be trusted.
IP Source Guard: stops hosts from using IP addresses not assigned to them via DHCP.
Storm control: prevents a broadcast storm from taking down the entire segment — sets threshold (packets/sec or %).

items.title: ACLs and 802.1X / NAC
items.body:
ACCESS CONTROL LISTS (ACLs):
  Standard ACL: matches SOURCE IP only. Numbered 1–99 or 1300–1999.
  Extended ACL: matches src IP + dst IP + protocol + src/dst port. Numbered 100–199 or 2000–2699.

  PLACEMENT RULE:
    Extended ACL → as CLOSE to SOURCE as possible (blocks traffic early)
    Standard ACL → as CLOSE to DESTINATION as possible (only matches src IP, so must be near dest to avoid over-blocking)

  ACL PROCESSING:
    Top-down, first-match wins. Implicit deny at end = any traffic not explicitly permitted is dropped.
    Always add explicit 'permit ip any any' at bottom if you want to allow everything else.

802.1X PORT-BASED ACCESS CONTROL:
  Supplicant (client) → Authenticator (switch/AP) → Authentication Server (RADIUS)
  EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) is the framework used.
  Port starts in unauthorised state — only 802.1X traffic allowed.
  On RADIUS Accept: port moves to authorised state — full network access granted.
  On RADIUS Reject: port stays blocked (or placed in guest VLAN if configured).

NAC (Network Access Control):
  Checks endpoint posture before granting network access — is antivirus up to date? Patches current? Compliant?
  Non-compliant endpoints quarantined to remediation VLAN.
key_points: Standard ACL near destination. Extended ACL near source.
Implicit deny: last rule in every ACL — drops anything not matched above. Often the reason traffic is blocked.
802.1X requires: supplicant (client + EAP software), authenticator (switch with 802.1X enabled), RADIUS server.
NAC = posture assessment before access. Quarantine VLAN for non-compliant hosts.
ACL numbers: standard = 1–99. Extended = 100–199. Named ACLs also supported.
ACE (Access Control Entry): individual line in an ACL. Processed top to bottom — order matters.

objectives.name: The Methodology
objectives.description: CompTIA's 7-step troubleshooting process, OSI layer approaches, and problem documentation.

items.title: CompTIA 7-Step Troubleshooting Methodology
rows: Gather info from user, identify symptoms, duplicate the problem, question obvious changes, check logs
Establish a theory of probable cause
Consider obvious causes first (OSI bottom-up or top-down, or divide & conquer)
Confirm or deny the theory with specific tests. If confirmed → step 4. If wrong → back to step 2.
Document the fix, consider impact, identify side effects, get approval if needed
Apply the fix. Escalate if beyond skill level or authority.
Test that the reported problem is resolved AND that nothing else broke
Record: problem, root cause, fix applied, lessons learned. Update documentation.
key_points: MEMORISE the 7 steps in order — exam questions often ask what comes next.
Step 1: ALWAYS question what has changed recently — most problems follow a change.
Step 3: if theory is wrong, go back to step 2 — do NOT skip straight to implementing a fix.
Step 6: verify the fix AND check for side effects (fixing one thing can break another).
Step 7: documentation is mandatory — not optional. Records help future troubleshooting.
Escalation happens at step 5 if the technician lacks authority or expertise to fix it.

items.title: Troubleshooting Approaches
rows: Start at Physical layer — check cables, NIC, power
Physical symptoms obvious: cable unplugged, link light off, interface errors
Start at Application layer — can the app connect?
Application-specific problem: one app broken, others work fine
Start at Layer 3 (ping gateway, ping DNS) — split the problem
Problem location unknown — rapidly narrow scope by testing mid-stack first
Trace the traffic path from source to destination step by step
Intermittent issues, routing problems, asymmetric paths
Compare current metrics against known-good baseline
Degraded performance (not total failure) — spot what changed
Replace suspect component with known-good spare
Hardware suspected — quickest way to isolate NIC, cable, SFP
key_points: Bottom-up: most systematic. Good for physical issues. Can be slow if problem is at Layer 7.
Divide and conquer: most efficient in practice — ping the gateway first to establish Layer 3 works.
Ping test sequence: loopback (127.0.0.1) → own IP → gateway → remote IP → DNS name.
If ping IP works but DNS name fails → DNS problem, not network connectivity.
If ping gateway fails but ping own IP works → local config issue (wrong mask, wrong gateway).
Document the approach used — helps next engineer start where you left off.

items.title: The 7-Step Mnemonic — "Ice Eaters Taste Everything In Vivid Detail"
items.body:
Ice Eaters Taste Everything In Vivid Detail = I-E-T-E-I-V-D, the 7 steps in order:
Identify → Establish theory → Test theory → Establish plan → Implement (or escalate) → Verify → Document.

If step 3 (Test) fails, loop back to step 2 — don't skip ahead to a fix.
key_points: Step 3 fails → back to step 2, never jump straight to implementing.
Step 5: escalate if the fix is beyond your skill or authority.
Step 6: verify the FIX, and check nothing else broke.
Step 7: documenting is mandatory, not optional.

objectives.name: The Cable Lab
objectives.description: Physical layer faults, cable types, connectors, and troubleshooting tools.

items.title: Cable Types & Pinouts
rows: Same standard (T568B or T568A) on BOTH ends
PC → switch, switch → router (different device types)
T568A on one end, T568B on other end
PC → PC, switch → switch direct (same device types). MDI/MDIX auto-negates this on modern equipment.
Pins reversed (pin 1↔8, 2↔7, etc.) — flat ribbon cable
Laptop serial/USB → router/switch console port for CLI management
W/G, G, W/Or, Bl, W/Bl, Or, W/Br, Br
Used in government buildings, some home installations
W/Or, Or, W/G, Bl, W/Bl, G, W/Br, Br
Most common in commercial/enterprise wiring in North America
key_points: T568B is the dominant standard in enterprise — most patch panels and wall jacks use T568B.
T568A vs T568B: only orange and green pairs swap. Both are valid — just must be consistent.
Split pair: wires from different pairs twisted together — looks correct on continuity test but fails due to crosstalk. Requires proper wire map tester to detect.
MDI/MDIX auto-sensing: modern switches auto-detect cable type — crossover cables rarely needed today.
Rollover cable: pins completely reversed (1↔8). Used ONLY for console/management access, not data.
Open circuit: wire broken — no connectivity. Short circuit: two wires touching — both fail.

items.title: Physical Layer Troubleshooting Tools
rows: Verifies all 8 wires are connected and in correct order (wire map)
Quickly validate a patch cable or horizontal run — finds opens, shorts, reversed pairs
Toner injects audio tone; probe detects tone to trace cable through walls/bundles
Locate which cable in a bundle goes where; trace cables with no labels
Sends light pulse into fiber; measures reflections to locate breaks/faults and measure distance
Fiber troubleshooting — exact location of a break, splice quality, end-to-end loss mapping
Measures optical power (dBm) at the end of a fiber run
Verify fiber meets loss budget; confirm signal strong enough for the transceiver
Injects visible red light into fiber — light visible at break point or bend
Quickly find breaks, tight bends, or bad connectors on short fiber runs
Test power supplies, verify cable continuity, check for opens/shorts on copper
Connects TX to RX on a port — tests the port's ability to send and receive
Verify NIC/switch port hardware works; isolate port vs cable vs device issue
Seats wire into IDC (Insulation Displacement Connector) on patch panels/keystones
Terminating horizontal cable runs at patch panels and wall jacks
Shows RF energy across frequency bands — identifies interference sources
Wireless troubleshooting — find rogue APs, microwave interference, baby monitors on 2.4GHz
key_points: OTDR is the key fiber tool — finds exact location of a break (reports distance in meters/feet).
Toner probe (fox and hound): toner at one end, probe at other — traces unknown cables through walls.
Optical power meter: measures dBm. Know expected loss values for the fiber type/length.
Loopback test: if loopback passes but cable fails → cable is the problem. If loopback fails → port/NIC is the problem.
Spectrum analyser for wireless: identifies non-Wi-Fi interference (microwave = 2.4GHz broadband noise).
Cable certifier (high-end tester): not just continuity — measures attenuation, crosstalk, return loss to certify Cat6A 10GbE compliance.

items.title: Common Cable Faults
rows: Broken conductor inside the cable or at a connector
Continuity tester — fail on affected pair
Continuity tester — continuity between wrong pins
Incorrect wiring — T568A one end, B other when straight needed
No link (if MDIX not supported) or works on modern switches with MDIX
Wires from different pairs twisted together (e.g., pin 1 from pair 2)
Passes continuity test but high crosstalk — data errors at speed
Wire map tester with pair identification
Signal weakens over distance — exceeding 100m or poor quality cable
Intermittent errors, reduced speed, link may drop
Interference between adjacent pairs in same cable
High error rates, especially at Gigabit speeds
External electromagnetic or radio interference (motors, fluorescent lights)
CRC errors, increased collisions, intermittent outages
Move cable away from power lines; use STP (shielded)
key_points: Split pairs PASS a simple continuity test (all 8 wires connected) but FAIL a wire map test — critical difference.
Attenuation: worst on long runs. Keep horizontal cable ≤90m (100m total with patch cables).
Crosstalk: reduces with proper twist density. Untwisting more than 0.5 inches at termination causes NEXT.
EMI: run data cables perpendicular to power cables when crossing; avoid running parallel and close.
Shielded cable (STP/FTP): required near high-EMI sources — requires proper grounding to be effective.

items.title: dB Math — The Rule of 10s and 3s
items.body:
dB is logarithmic, but two shortcuts cover most exam math:
±10dB = ×10 or ÷10 power.
±3dB = ×2 or ÷2 power.

Example: -13dB loss = -10dB (÷10) then -3dB (÷2) = original power ÷20.
key_points: +dB = gain (amp/repeater). -dB = loss (attenuation, splices, connectors).
Typical loss: ~0.3-0.5dB per connector, ~0.1-0.2dB per splice.
Power meter reads dBm — compare against the transceiver's minimum receive sensitivity.
Add up all losses (connectors + splices + fiber length) and check against the link's dB budget.

objectives.name: The Command Post
objectives.description: Network troubleshooting commands — ping, traceroute, nslookup, nmap, netstat, arp, ipconfig.

items.title: Troubleshooting Commands — Quick Reference
rows: Tests ICMP reachability to a host; measures RTT
Reply vs Request timeout (no route/blocked/down); TTL value; RTT ms
Shows hop-by-hop path to destination with RTT at each hop
Where * * * appear (timeout/blocked); high RTT at specific hop; last hop before failure
Combines ping + traceroute — shows packet loss % at each hop
Loss% column — identifies which hop drops packets
Shows NIC IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, MAC, DNS
169.254.x.x = APIPA (no DHCP); wrong mask; missing gateway
Queries DNS — resolves hostnames to IPs or looks up records
NXDOMAIN = name not found; wrong IP returned = DNS issue; which server answered
Shows ARP cache — IP-to-MAC mappings learned by the local host
Duplicate IP: two entries with same IP different MACs; wrong gateway MAC
Shows active network connections, listening ports, routing table
netstat -an: open ports/connections; netstat -r: routing table
Network discovery and port scanning — finds open ports, OS fingerprinting
Open/closed/filtered ports; host discovery on subnet
Displays routing table — shows all routes the OS knows
Missing default gateway; wrong next-hop; unreachable network
Shows interface status, speed/duplex, error counters
Input errors, CRC, runts, giants; line up/protocol down vs both down
Shows routing table — connected, static, and dynamic routes
Missing network; wrong AD; default route (0.0.0.0/0) present or absent
Shows ARP table on router/switch — IP-to-MAC mappings
Incomplete ARP entry; wrong MAC for a gateway IP
key_points: 169.254.x.x in ipconfig/ifconfig = APIPA — host failed to get a DHCP address.
ping 127.0.0.1 = loopback test. If this fails → TCP/IP stack broken on the local machine.
traceroute: * * * at a hop = that router blocks ICMP TTL-exceeded. Not always a problem — check if NEXT hop responds.
nslookup: always check which DNS server responded — client may be pointing at wrong DNS.
arp -a: if gateway MAC resolves to attacker's MAC → ARP poisoning. If incomplete → ARP failing (Layer 2 issue).
netstat -rn: routing table without DNS resolution — faster. Shows if default route (0.0.0.0) is present.

items.title: netstat Connection States — Reading the Conversation
items.body:
LISTENING = a service is waiting, but not yet talking to anyone.
ESTABLISHED = an active session — both sides exchanging data.
TIME_WAIT = connection just closed, OS holding the socket briefly to catch stray packets.
CLOSE_WAIT = remote side closed, but THIS host hasn't closed its end — often an app bug.
key_points: Many LISTENING ports with nothing ESTABLISHED → service up, but no clients connecting.
Lots of CLOSE_WAIT → app isn't closing sockets — possible resource leak.
TIME_WAIT pile-up under load is normal — it self-clears after the OS timeout.
netstat -an: -a = all connections/listening ports, -n = numeric (no DNS lookups).

items.title: Connectivity Decision Flow (isolate the fault)
items.body:
Work outward from the host:

  ping 127.0.0.1 (loopback) fails -> TCP/IP stack broken on THIS host
  ping own IP fails          -> NIC / driver issue
  ping default gateway fails -> local link / switch / cabling / VLAN
  ping remote IP fails (gw OK) -> routing / remote-side issue
  ping by NAME fails, by IP works -> DNS problem
key_points: Name fails + IP works = DNS. The #1 'connected but can't browse' cause.
169.254.x.x = APIPA = DHCP failed (no lease).
Reach gateway but not internet = routing / ISP / upstream issue.
traceroute shows WHERE the path dies; pathping shows packet-loss % per hop.

objectives.name: The Signal Tower
objectives.description: Wireless troubleshooting — interference, coverage, authentication failures, and APIPA.

items.title: Wireless Troubleshooting Scenarios
rows: AP too far away; SSID broadcasting disabled; wrong frequency band (5GHz device looking for 2.4GHz)
Move closer; enable SSID broadcast; check band compatibility
DHCP failure — AP DHCP scope exhausted or DHCP server unreachable
Renew DHCP (ipconfig /release /renew); check DHCP server; check DHCP scope
2.4GHz interference — microwave operates in 2.4GHz ISM band
Move client to 5GHz band (SSID); change AP channel to 1, 6, or 11
Co-channel interference (nearby APs on same channel); high client count; background noise
Change channel; reduce AP transmit power for smaller cells; add APs
Re-enter passphrase carefully; check WPA2/WPA3 mode matches
RADIUS server unreachable; wrong certificate; client EAP type mismatch
Verify RADIUS reachability; check cert validity; match EAP profile on client and server
CAPWAP tunnel to WLC broken; AP not getting IP from DHCP; AP not provisioned in WLC
Check WLC CAPWAP connectivity; verify AP gets DHCP; check WLC AP whitelist
AP cells not overlapping adequately (coverage gap)
Increase transmit power or add AP; ensure 15-20% cell overlap for roaming
key_points: 169.254.x.x (APIPA) on wireless = DHCP problem, not wireless problem. The wireless connected successfully.
2.4GHz interference sources: microwave ovens, Bluetooth, baby monitors, cordless phones, ZigBee devices.
Co-channel interference worse than adjacent-channel. Always use channels 1, 6, 11 on 2.4GHz.
Signal strength (dBm) vs signal quality: strong signal with high noise floor = still poor quality.
Hidden SSID: client must manually enter SSID name — provides minimal security benefit, causes connection issues.
Band steering: AP can push capable clients to 5GHz to reduce 2.4GHz congestion.

items.title: Reading Wi-Fi Signal — dBm and SNR
items.body:
dBm is negative — closer to 0 is stronger:
-30dBm = excellent (right next to the AP).
-67dBm = usable minimum for VoIP/video.
-80dBm or worse = unreliable, frequent retries.

SNR = signal minus noise floor. Below ~20dB means low speeds even if the signal looks 'strong'.
key_points: A strong signal (-40dBm) on a noisy channel can perform worse than a weaker, quiet one.
Roaming threshold: clients should switch APs around -67 to -70dBm, not wait for -80dBm.
RSSI scales differ by vendor — compare trends, not raw numbers, across devices.
High noise floor = more retransmits = lower throughput, even with full bars.

items.title: 2.4 vs 5 vs 6 GHz — the range/speed trade-off
items.body:
2.4 GHz - longest range, best through walls, but only 3 non-overlapping
            channels (1, 6, 11) and crowded (microwave, Bluetooth).
  5 GHz   - many channels, far less interference, higher throughput,
            but shorter range and weaker through walls.
  6 GHz   - most spectrum, least congestion, shortest range (Wi-Fi 6E).

More range <-> less speed/cleaner air. Always a trade-off.
key_points: 2.4 GHz non-overlapping channels: 1, 6, 11. Memorize them.
Microwave/Bluetooth interference -> it's 2.4 GHz -> move to 5 GHz.
Co-channel interference = too many APs sharing one channel.
Far from AP / through walls -> 2.4 GHz reaches better than 5 GHz.

items.title: Common Network Service Issues
rows: Host gets 169.254.x.x IP — cannot reach network
DHCP server unreachable, scope exhausted, or DHCP disabled
ipconfig /release /renew; check DHCP server; expand scope
New devices cannot get IP addresses
All IPs in DHCP scope assigned; stale leases not released
Expand scope; reduce lease time; clean stale leases
Host gets IP but cannot route outside local subnet
DHCP option 3 (default gateway) misconfigured in scope
Correct gateway IP in DHCP scope options
Host gets IP and can ping IPs but cannot resolve names
Correct DNS server IP in DHCP scope options
Hostname lookup fails — NXDOMAIN error in nslookup
DNS record doesn't exist; wrong DNS server queried; split-brain DNS issue
Add missing DNS record; verify client is querying correct DNS server
Browser goes to wrong site; ping resolves wrong address
Stale DNS cache; DNS poisoning; wrong A record in DNS
ipconfig /flushdns; check DNS record; verify DNSSEC
Intermittent connectivity for one or both hosts; ARP conflicts
Two devices configured with same static IP; static IP in DHCP pool
Find and fix duplicate; exclude static IPs from DHCP pool
Can ping local hosts but cannot reach internet or other subnets
Default gateway IP wrong or missing in host config or DHCP scope
Fix gateway IP in host config or DHCP scope
Can only reach some hosts on what appears to be the same LAN
Subnet mask set too large or too small — host computes wrong network range
Correct subnet mask; check DHCP scope mask option
Kerberos auth failures; certificate errors; log timestamp mismatch
NTP server unreachable; wrong NTP server IP; firewall blocks UDP 123
Fix NTP server address; open UDP 123; verify NTP hierarchy
key_points: APIPA 169.254.x.x: Windows/macOS assign this when DHCP fails — means DHCP is broken, not the NIC.
ipconfig /release then /renew: forces DHCP rebind — quick fix for lease issues.
ipconfig /flushdns: clears local DNS cache — fixes stale or poisoned cached entries.
Duplicate IP: ARP conflict causes both hosts to drop off the network intermittently.
NTP failure causes Kerberos auth to fail (5-minute clock skew tolerance in Active Directory).
Wrong subnet mask: host A at 192.168.1.1/24 and host B at 192.168.1.1/25 may not communicate if mask mismatches cause incorrect network calculations.

items.title: IP Addressing Diagnostic Flow
items.body:
SYSTEMATIC PING TEST SEQUENCE:
  Step 1: ping 127.0.0.1 (loopback)
    FAIL → TCP/IP stack is broken on local machine

  Step 2: ping <own IP address>
    FAIL → NIC driver issue or duplicate IP conflict

  Step 3: ping <default gateway>
    FAIL → check IP/mask/gateway config; check cable/switch; ARP cache
    → 'ping works but traceroute fails' often = ICMP blocked by firewall

  Step 4: ping <remote IP address>
    FAIL → routing issue between networks; check routing table (route print)

  Step 5: ping <hostname / FQDN>
    FAIL but Step 4 WORKS → DNS issue (nslookup to diagnose)
    FAIL and Step 4 FAILS → network connectivity issue

COMMON WRONG MASK SYMPTOMS:
  /24 instead of /25 → host thinks it's on a larger subnet, tries to ARP for hosts that are actually on another subnet
  /25 instead of /24 → host thinks some same-LAN hosts are remote, sends to gateway instead of direct

ROUTING TABLE CHECK:
  Missing default route (0.0.0.0/0) → can reach local subnet, nothing else
  Correct route present but wrong next-hop → traffic goes to wrong place
key_points: Loopback (127.0.0.1) ALWAYS responds if TCP/IP stack works — doesn't need a NIC.
APIPA means DHCP failed — not a DNS or firewall issue. Renew DHCP first.
Ping IP works, ping hostname fails → pure DNS issue. Check nslookup output.
Ping gateway fails → check: Is IP in same subnet as gateway? Is cable connected? ARP resolve?
route print (Windows) / ip route (Linux): default route shows as 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0.
ipconfig /all: shows ALL NIC info including DNS servers, DHCP lease time, MAC address.
